cards.q: How is the warehouse modelled?
cards.a: As a finite graph $$G=(V,E)$$. Vertices are the discrete positions a robot can occupy; edges are movements that are physically possible between adjacent positions. The formulation deliberately does not assume a lattice, because real warehouses have one-way aisles, diagonal shortcuts and irregular blocks.

cards.q: What are the four vertex roles, and are they really a "partition" of V?
cards.a: $$V_{mov}\subseteq V$$: vertices an agent may occupy. $$V_{str}\subseteq V_{mov}$$: storage faces (occupiable, since a pickup is completed by standing on $$s_j$$). $$V_{del}\subseteq V_{mov}$$: delivery/drop-off points (occupiable, same reason). $$V_{ep}\subseteq V_{mov}$$: endpoints, where an idle agent may wait without blocking transit. Not a true partition: $$V_{ep}$$ is a subset of $$V_{mov}$$, not disjoint from it, and $$V_{str},V_{del},V_{ep}$$ need not be pairwise disjoint either — "label" is the more accurate word.

cards.q: [Fix] The original text left $$V_{str}$$ and $$V_{del}$$ as merely $$\subseteq V$$, not $$\subseteq V_{mov}$$. Why was that a real gap, not just a style issue?
cards.a: Agents only ever occupy $$\ell_i(t)\in V_{mov}$$. If $$V_{str}$$/$$V_{del}$$ were disjoint from $$V_{mov}$$ — which "partition" suggested — an agent could never physically occupy a pickup or delivery vertex, leaving pickup/delivery undefined. The fix states $$V_{str},V_{del}\subseteq V_{mov}$$ explicitly.

cards.q: Is the warehouse graph $$G$$ directed or undirected, and what connectivity is assumed?
cards.a: Directed — one-way aisles mean $$(v,w)\in E$$ need not imply $$(w,v)\in E$$, and the two directions may have different costs (this was implied by the swap-conflict notation but never stated outright). $$G$$ is assumed rich enough that $$d_G(v,w)$$ is finite for every vertex pair used in the formulation (e.g. every occupiable vertex can reach every target it's ever assigned); instances are checked against this.

cards.q: What does an edge carry, and what does $$d_G(v,w)$$ denote?
cards.a: Each edge $$e\in E$$ carries a traversal cost $$c(e) > 0$$. $$d_G(v,w)$$ is the shortest-path cost from $$v$$ to $$w$$.

cards.q: Define the action set $$\mathcal{U}(v)$$ available at vertex $$v$$.
cards.a: $$\mathcal{U}(v) = \{\mathrm{wait}\} \cup \{\mathrm{move}(w) : w \in N^{+}(v)\}$$, where $$N^{+}(v) = \{w \in V_{mov} : (v,w) \in E\}$$ are the movable successors of $$v$$.

cards.q: Give the realised one-step cost $$\hat{c}(v,w)$$.
cards.a: $$\hat{c}(v,w) = c_{wait}$$ if $$v=w$$ (waiting), and $$\hat{c}(v,w) = c(v,w)$$ if $$(v,w)\in E$$ (moving).

cards.q: Why must the one-step cost be split into two cases instead of just using $$c(v,v)$$ for waiting?
cards.a: Because a self-loop $$(v,v)$$ is not an element of $$E$$, so $$c$$ is undefined for it. Without the piecewise definition, any route cost containing a wait would be ill-typed.

cards.q: What determines whether an agent prefers to yield or to detour around a conflict?
cards.a: The value of $$c_{wait}$$ relative to edge costs. It is treated as a parameter of the study, not a fixed constant of the model.

cards.q: What is the "well-formed instance" assumption, and how is it used?
cards.a: At least $$m$$ non-task endpoints exist, and between any pair of endpoints there is a path avoiding a third endpoint. It is imposed on generated instances as an assumption (not derived), and is only reported for the baselines that require completeness on well-formed instances.

cards.q: What is the fleet $$\mathcal{A}$$, and what does agent $$a_i$$ select at time $$t$$?
cards.a: $$\mathcal{A} = \{a_1,\dots,a_m\}$$, a set of homogeneous agents. Agent $$a_i$$ occupies $$\ell_i(t)\in V_{mov}$$ and selects an action $$u_i(t) \in \mathcal{U}(\ell_i(t))$$.

cards.q: When is a single agent's transition legal?
cards.a: $$\ell_i(t+1) = \ell_i(t) \;\vee\; (\ell_i(t), \ell_i(t+1)) \in E$$ — the agent either stays put or moves along an existing edge.

cards.q: State the vertex-conflict constraint.
cards.a: $$\ell_i(t+1) \neq \ell_j(t+1) \;\; \forall i \neq j$$ — no two agents may end a timestep at the same vertex.

cards.q: State the swap-conflict constraint.
cards.a: $$\neg\bigl(\ell_i(t) = \ell_j(t+1) \wedge \ell_j(t) = \ell_i(t+1)\bigr) \;\; \forall i \neq j$$ — no two agents may exchange positions across a single edge in one step.

cards.q: Why are the vertex-conflict and swap-conflict constraints logically independent?
cards.a: The vertex constraint inspects only the successor state at $$t+1$$. The swap constraint inspects the pair (state at $$t$$, state at $$t+1$$) and is invisible to any check performed only at $$t+1$$. Omitting it would let two agents pass through each other in a single-lane aisle.

cards.q: Why can't collision-freedom be enforced purely as a reward penalty for a learned policy?
cards.a: The constraints are hard feasibility conditions: a run that violates them is not a solution at all. A learned policy induces a distribution over joint actions whose support may contain infeasible ones, so a separate enforcement mechanism is required rather than relying on penalties to be learned away.

cards.q: Why does a collision-free joint action always exist?
cards.a: Because waiting is a legal action at every vertex for every agent, so in the worst case all conflicting agents can simply wait.

cards.q: How is the storage state $$x_t$$ defined, and why not a simpler mapping?
cards.a: As a counting function $$x_t : \mathcal{K}\times V_{str} \to \mathbb{N}_0$$, giving the number of units of SKU $$k$$ at storage vertex $$v$$. A simpler map $$\sigma_t : \mathcal{K}\to V_{str}$$ would force one location per SKU, unit quantity and unlimited shelf space — admissible only if stated explicitly.

cards.q: Define the feasible configuration set $$\mathcal{X}$$.
cards.a: $$\mathcal{X} = \{x \in \mathbb{N}_0^{|\mathcal{K}|\times|V_{str}|} : \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} b_k\, x(k,v) \le \mathrm{cap}(v) \;\; \forall v \in V_{str}\}$$, where $$b_k>0$$ is per-unit capacity use and $$\mathrm{cap}(v)>0$$ is vertex capacity.

cards.q: Why is $$\mathcal{X}$$ described as a system of knapsack constraints?
cards.a: There is one capacity constraint per storage vertex ($$|V_{str}|$$ total), and each couples the placement decisions of every SKU competing for that vertex's shared capacity.

cards.q: Give the storage update rule and explain why it is causal.
cards.a: $$x_t = F(x_{t-\Delta},\, \hat{\rho}_t,\, \hat{\mu}_t,\, \hat{w}_t) \in \mathcal{X}$$, applied at slow epochs $$t\in\{\Delta,2\Delta,\dots\}$$. It is causal because $$\hat\rho_t$$ (demand), $$\hat\mu_t$$ (traversal counts) and $$\hat w_t$$ (waiting) are estimated only from data available strictly before the epoch.

cards.q: [Fix] What was missing before this rule can even apply at $$t=\Delta$$, and how is it fixed?
cards.a: An initial storage configuration. $$x_t=F(x_{t-\Delta},\dots)$$ needs $$x_0$$ to bootstrap it, but $$x_0$$ was never introduced anywhere. Fix: $$x_0\in\mathcal{X}$$ is now stated explicitly as part of the problem instance.

cards.q: What is the fixed-storage baseline $$F_{fix}$$, and how is it defined?
cards.a: The identity rule $$F_{fix}(x,\cdot) = x$$ — defined directly as a rule, rather than as the informal limit $$\Delta = \infty$$.

cards.q: Formally, what is $$\mathcal{F}$$ (the space $$F$$ ranges over in the decision problem)?
cards.a: [Fix — originally undefined] The set of measurable functions $$F:\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{|\mathcal{K}|}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{|E|}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{|E|}\to\mathcal{X}$$ — taking a prior configuration plus the three estimates to a feasible configuration. $$F_{fix}\in\mathcal{F}$$ is one particular element.

cards.q: Write the storage objective and explain each term (D, K, R).
cards.a: $$x_t \in \arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}} [\alpha D(x;\hat\rho_t) + \beta K(x;\hat\mu_t,\hat w_t) + \chi R(x,x_{t-\Delta})]$$. $$D$$: demand-weighted access distance — popular items should be close. $$K$$: predicted congestion exposure — don't put them all on one corridor. $$R$$: reassignment penalty — don't rearrange every epoch.

cards.q: [Fix] Eq. 7 defines $$x_t=F(\dots)$$ as a function, but eq. 8 computes it via $$\arg\min$$. Why is that a problem, and how is it resolved?
cards.a: $$\arg\min$$ over a set can have multiple minimisers, i.e. be set-valued — so eq. 8 alone doesn't guarantee eq. 7 is well-defined as a genuine function. Fix: $$F$$ is required to apply a fixed tie-breaking rule over the minimising set (specified alongside the search heuristic in Method), so $$x_t$$ is always a single, well-defined value.

cards.q: Is the storage objective solved to optimality, and what happens when $$\chi=0$$?
cards.a: No — it is an integer program solved only by heuristic search (specified in the Method section). Setting $$\chi=0$$ removes relocation cost entirely, which is recorded as a limitation rather than treated as a minor simplification.

cards.q: Why can't the storage update be a per-item greedy score applied independently to each SKU?
cards.a: Because capacity constraints in $$\mathcal{X}$$ couple different SKUs placed at the same vertex, making the update a joint constrained decision over $$\mathcal{X}$$, not a set of independent per-item choices.

cards.q: What is a task $$\tau_j$$, formally?
cards.a: A quadruple $$\tau_j = (r_j, s_j, g_j, k_j)$$: release time $$r_j\in\mathbb{N}_0$$, pickup vertex $$s_j\in V_{str}$$, delivery vertex $$g_j\in V_{del}$$, requested SKU $$k_j\in\mathcal{K}$$.

cards.q: [Fix] Why did the task tuple need a fourth component $$k_j$$ added?
cards.a: The original tuple was only $$(r_j,s_j,g_j)$$, but the coupling condition immediately after it uses $$k_j$$ (the requested SKU) without ever defining it — the thesis's central equation rested on an undefined symbol. Adding $$k_j\in\mathcal{K}$$ to the tuple itself closes the gap.

cards.q: What generates tasks, and what does $$\lambda_{task}$$ mean?
cards.a: Orders are drawn each timestep from a distribution $$P_{ord}$$ (a finite multiset of SKU–quantity pairs) and converted into tasks by a task-generation rule. $$\lambda_{task}$$ is the expected number of tasks released per timestep.

cards.q: State the coupling condition, and explain why it is the central object of the thesis.
cards.a: $$x_{r_j}(k_j, s_j) > 0$$ — the pickup vertex must actually hold stock of the requested SKU at release. It is the formal link between the two layers: it makes the spatial location of pickups a function of the storage configuration, so any change to $$x_t$$ changes the routing problem the controller subsequently faces.

cards.q: What are the three disjoint sets a task passes through over its life, and when does a task move between them?
cards.a: Waiting set $$\mathcal{Q}_t$$ (entered at release), active set $$\mathcal{B}_t$$ (entered at assignment), completed set $$\mathcal{C}_t$$ (entered at delivery). The convention used throughout: execution begins at assignment, not when the agent physically arrives at $$s_j$$.

cards.q: [Fix] $$\mathcal{Q}_t,\mathcal{B}_t,\mathcal{C}_t$$ were only described narratively, with disjointness just asserted. What is the formal fix, and what new symbol does it need?
cards.a: Introduce the assignment time $$y_j$$ (with $$r_j\le y_j\le d_j$$), then define $$\mathcal{Q}_t=\{\tau_j: r_j\le t<y_j\}$$, $$\mathcal{B}_t=\{\tau_j: y_j\le t<d_j\}$$, $$\mathcal{C}_t=\{\tau_j: d_j\le t\}$$. Disjointness now *follows* from the three half-open intervals partitioning $$[r_j,\infty)$$, instead of being a separately asserted runtime property.

cards.q: Define service time $$\zeta_j$$, and explain why a controller cannot improve it by delaying assignment.
cards.a: $$\zeta_j = d_j - r_j$$. It spans both the waiting phase and the active phase, so postponing assignment only shifts time between phases — it cannot shorten the total.

cards.q: If inventory depletion and replenishment are not simulated, how should $$x_t$$ be interpreted?
cards.a: As a placement template rather than a physical inventory level — it says where items are considered to be for generating pickups, not a stock count that depletes.

cards.q: What two logically distinct jobs does a controller $$\pi$$ perform?
cards.a: Task assignment (mapping free agents and waiting tasks to agent–task pairs) and routing (mapping the resulting targets and available information to actions $$u_i(t)\in\mathcal{U}(\ell_i(t))$$). Both are treated as part of $$\pi$$.

cards.q: [Fix] Formally, what is $$\Pi$$ (the space $$\pi$$ ranges over in the decision problem)?
cards.a: [Originally undefined — only "what info it may condition on" was given] $$\Pi$$ is the set of pairs $$\pi=(\pi^{assign},\pi^{route})$$: $$\pi^{route}$$ maps the information allowed under a regime (Table I) to a joint action in $$\prod_i \mathcal{U}(\ell_i(t))$$; $$\pi^{assign}$$ maps free agents and $$\mathcal{Q}_t$$ to a partial matching. Table I constrains only the argument each map may depend on, nothing else.

cards.q: What is the single distinction between the three controller architectures studied?
cards.a: What information each component (assignment, routing) is permitted to condition on — nothing else about the problem changes between them.

cards.q: Describe the centralised architecture.
cards.a: Both assignment and routing may condition on the full global state.

cards.q: Describe the section-based architecture, including the zone partition.
cards.a: Movable vertices are split into disjoint zones $$\mathcal{Y}=\{Y_1,\dots,Y_p\}$$ with $$\bigcup_q Y_q = V_{mov}$$ and $$Y_q \cap Y_{q'} = \emptyset$$ for $$q\neq q'$$. Assignment and routing condition only on zone-local information, plus an explicit protocol at zone boundaries.

cards.q: Describe the decentralised architecture.
cards.a: Routing conditions only on the local observation via a shared parameterised policy $$u_i(t) \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid o_i(t))$$. Assignment still uses the global state, held fixed across arms so it isn't a confound.

cards.q: What does "centralised training with decentralised execution" (CTDE) mean here?
cards.a: Global information may be used during training only. Parameter sharing across homogeneous agents does not, by itself, make execution centralised.

cards.q: Why is task assignment held identical across all three architectures?
cards.a: So that any difference in experimental results can be attributed to the routing architecture alone, rather than being confounded with differences in assignment quality.

cards.q: Define the depth-$$d$$ visible vertex set and induced subgraph for agent $$i$$.
cards.a: $$V_i^{(d)}(t) = \{v \in V_{mov} : d_G(\ell_i(t), v) \le d\}$$, and $$\mathcal{G}_i^{(d)}(t) = G[V_i^{(d)}(t)]$$, the subgraph induced by that vertex set.

cards.q: Why is it useful that the observation size is bounded independently of $$|V|$$, and what is the price?
cards.a: It allows a single trained policy to be evaluated on warehouses larger than those it trained on. The price: anything beyond $$d$$ hops is invisible, so an agent may commit to a move that only becomes a conflict a few steps later.

cards.q: Define the target-distance potential $$\eta_i(v,t)$$, and what property makes it a potential?
cards.a: $$\eta_i(v,t) = d_G(v, q_i(t))$$, the distance from $$v$$ to the agent's current target $$q_i(t)$$. By the triangle inequality, $$\eta_i(w,t)-\eta_i(v,t) \ge -c(v,w)$$ for every edge $$(v,w)$$, with **equality iff** $$(v,w)$$ lies on a shortest path to $$q_i(t)$$.

cards.q: [Math error fixed] The original claim was "$$\eta_i(w,t)-\eta_i(v,t)$$ is negative exactly on shortest-path moves." Why is that false, with a concrete counterexample?
cards.a: Negative is necessary but not sufficient for a shortest-path move. Counterexample: $$c(v,w)=1$$, $$d_G(v,q)=5$$, and some other route gives $$d_G(w,q)=4.5$$. The difference is $$4.5-5=-0.5$$ (negative), but $$(v,w)$$ is NOT on a shortest path — that would require $$d_G(w,q)=4$$ exactly (equality with $$-c(v,w)=-1$$). A negative difference shows *progress*, not *optimality*.

cards.q: How does $$\eta_i$$ let congestion avoidance be expressed as a local trade-off?
cards.a: Following an edge that attains equality in $$\eta_i(w,t)-\eta_i(v,t)=-c(v,w)$$ realises the shortest path; congestion avoidance is the choice to accept a smaller decrease of $$\eta_i$$ (or even a non-negative step) now, in exchange for a lower expected total cost later.

cards.q: Define the local congestion feature $$\delta_i(t)$$, and where does it belong in the formulation?
cards.a: For congestion radius $$r_{cng}$$ (a separate parameter from observation depth $$d$$ and comms radius $$r_{com}$$), and excluding the agent itself: $$\delta_i(t) = \dfrac{|\{a_j\in\mathcal{A}\setminus\{a_i\}: \ell_j(t)\in V_i^{(r_{cng})}(t)\}|}{\max\{1,\,|V_i^{(r_{cng})}(t)|-1\}}$$. [Fix: originally defined later in the Learning Problem section but never added to $$o_i(t)$$ — it's an observation-layer quantity and now lives here, wired into the observation tuple below.]

cards.q: Define the communication graph $$G_t^{\mathcal{A}}$$, and how does it differ from the environment graph $$G$$?
cards.a: $$G_t^{\mathcal{A}} = (\mathcal{A}, E_t^{\mathcal{A}})$$ with $$(a_i,a_j)\in E_t^{\mathcal{A}} \iff i\neq j \wedge d_G(\ell_i(t),\ell_j(t)) \le r_{com}$$. Unlike $$G$$, its nodes are agents (not locations), it has a different cardinality, and its edges mean "can exchange information with" rather than "can move to" — the two must never be conflated.

cards.q: What four components make up the full observation $$o_i(t)$$?
cards.a: $$o_i(t) = (\mathcal{G}_i^{(d)}(t),\; \eta_i(\cdot,t),\; \delta_i(t),\; \text{messages from } \{a_j : (a_i,a_j)\in E_t^{\mathcal{A}}\})$$ — the local induced subgraph, the target-distance annotation, the congestion feature, and messages from agents within communication range. [Fix: $$\delta_i(t)$$ added — it was previously undefined in $$o_i(t)$$ despite being used as if part of the agent's local information.]

cards.q: What formal model is the decentralised setting cast as, and why?
cards.a: A partially observable stochastic game (POSG), because each agent acts from its own partial observation $$o_i(t)$$ while the environment evolves under the joint action of all agents.

cards.q: Write the POSG tuple $$\mathcal{M}$$ and name each component.
cards.a: $$\mathcal{M} = (\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{S}, \{\mathcal{U}_i\}_{i=1}^m, P, \{\mathcal{O}_i\}_{i=1}^m, \{O_i\}_{i=1}^m, \{R_i\}_{i=1}^m, \gamma)$$: agents, state space, action sets, transition kernel, observation spaces, observation functions, reward functions, discount factor.

cards.q: What is the difference between $$\mathcal{O}_i$$ and $$O_i$$ in the POSG?
cards.a: $$\mathcal{O}_i$$ is the observation space (the set of possible observations); $$O_i$$ is the observation function that maps the state to an observation for agent $$i$$.

cards.q: What is the type signature of the reward function $$R_i$$?
cards.a: $$R_i : \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{U}^m \times \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}$$ — it depends on the state, the full joint action, and the resulting next state.

cards.q: [Fix] $$\mathcal{U}(v)$$ is vertex-dependent (eq. 1), but the POSG tuple lists a fixed $$\mathcal{U}_i$$ per agent. How are these reconciled?
cards.a: [Originally never reconciled] Define $$\mathcal{U}_i := \bigcup_{v\in V_{mov}} \mathcal{U}(v)$$ — the union over all vertices. At a state where $$\ell_i(t)=v$$, only $$\mathcal{U}(v)\subseteq\mathcal{U}_i$$ is enabled; the rest of $$\mathcal{U}_i$$ gets probability zero under $$P$$ (action masking). This is how a vertex-dependent action set is embedded in a POSG's fixed per-agent action space.

cards.q: The congestion feature $$\delta_i(t)$$ is now defined in the Observations topic as part of $$o_i(t)$$ — what is its role here in the learning problem?
cards.a: Since $$\delta_i(t)$$ is part of $$o_i(t)$$, it is available both to the policy $$\pi_\theta$$ and to a reward designer; it may be used when $$R_i$$ is concretely realised in the Method section. [Fix: previously defined here with no formal connection to $$o_i(t)$$ or $$R_i$$ at all.]

cards.q: Why is the learning objective stated at team level rather than per agent?
cards.a: Because the agents are homogeneous, cooperative and share a single parameter vector $$\theta$$: $$\max_\theta J(\theta) = \max_\theta \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m R_i(t)\bigr]$$.

cards.q: [Fix] $$\theta$$ was only introduced for the decentralised architecture. Does $$J(\theta)$$ apply to the centralised/section-based regimes too?
cards.a: Yes, now stated explicitly: $$J(\theta)$$ applies to whichever of the three regimes (Table I) is realised as a learned controller, with $$\theta$$ ranging over that regime's own parameters — e.g. decentralised shared weights, or a centralised policy's global parameters.

cards.q: Why are the reward functions $$R_i$$ left unspecified in the problem formulation?
cards.a: A reward is only an instrument for obtaining a policy that scores well on the system-level criterion; it can be redesigned without changing the underlying problem, so its concrete form is deferred to the Method section.

cards.q: What two clocks does the system run on?
cards.a: A fast clock, advancing every timestep under the controller ($$s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot\mid s_t,u_t)$$), and a slow clock, applying the storage update only at epochs every $$\Delta$$ steps.

cards.q: What is the forward direction of the loop between storage and routing?
cards.a: A change in $$x_t$$ changes which vertices appear as pickups (via the coupling condition), which changes the routing problem the controller must solve.

cards.q: What is the backward direction of the loop?
cards.a: Realised routing statistics — traversal counts $$\mu_t$$ and waiting $$w_t$$ — feed into the next storage update through the rule $$F$$.

cards.q: In terms of the loop diagram, what exactly is the fixed-storage baseline?
cards.a: Exactly the same two-timescale diagram with the backward (feedback) arrow removed — the experimental contrast of the thesis is this diagram with and without that one arrow.

cards.q: What is the trade-off in choosing the storage epoch length $$\Delta$$?
cards.a: Too small: $$F$$ reacts to noise in the fast process, making the task distribution non-stationary from the learner's point of view. Too large: the estimates $$\hat\rho, \hat\mu, \hat w$$ become stale. Hence $$\Delta$$ is treated as an experimental variable, not a fixed constant.

cards.q: Define throughput $$\Lambda_T$$ and mean service time $$\bar\zeta_T$$.
cards.a: $$\Lambda_T = \dfrac{|\mathcal{C}_T|}{T}$$, and $$\bar\zeta_T = \dfrac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_T|}\sum_{\tau_j\in\mathcal{C}_T}(d_j - r_j)$$, over the completed set $$\mathcal{C}_T$$ across horizon $$T$$.

cards.q: Define movement cost per completed task $$\bar{c}_T$$.
cards.a: $$\bar{c}_T = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \hat{c}(\ell_i(t),\ell_i(t+1))}{|\mathcal{C}_T|}$$ — total realised travel cost of every agent, divided by the number of completed tasks.

cards.q: Why are runs with $$|\mathcal{C}_T|=0$$ reported separately rather than plugged into these formulas?
cards.a: Because the ratios (throughput, service time, movement cost) are undefined or meaningless with zero completions, rather than being assigned an arbitrary value.

cards.q: What is always reported alongside throughput and service time, and why?
cards.a: The backlog $$|\mathcal{Q}_T| + |\mathcal{B}_T|$$ and the age distribution of unfinished tasks — because a completion-only statistic can look good even while the system is quietly falling behind.

cards.q: Define the normalised entropy $$H_T$$ of edge usage, and what its extreme values mean.
cards.a: With $$p_T(e) = \mu_T(e) / \sum_{e'\in E}\mu_T(e')$$ over edges $$E_T^+$$ with traffic, $$H_T = -\dfrac{1}{\log|E_T^+|}\sum_{e\in E_T^+} p_T(e)\log p_T(e) \in [0,1]$$ (defined for $$|E_T^+|>1$$). $$H_T = 1$$ means perfectly uniform edge usage; $$H_T \to 0$$ means almost all traffic on one edge.

cards.q: [Fix] The entropy formula is only defined for $$|E_T^+|>1$$. What happens at the boundary ($$|E_T^+|\in\{0,1\}$$), and why was that a gap?
cards.a: $$\log|E_T^+|=0$$ when $$|E_T^+|=1$$, so the formula divides by zero — undefined, with no convention given originally. Fix: by convention $$H_T:=0$$ (so $$C_T:=1$$) when $$|E_T^+|=1$$ (usage is maximally concentrated on one edge); $$|E_T^+|=0$$ (no traversals) is reported separately, exactly like $$|\mathcal{C}_T|=0$$.

cards.q: Define the concentration index $$C_T$$, and why is it used with this sign rather than $$H_T$$ directly?
cards.a: $$C_T = 1 - H_T$$. The system-level criterion is minimised, so adding $$+H_T$$ would reward funnelling all traffic down a single aisle (low entropy is bad, but the term needs to grow with badness); $$C_T$$ grows as usage becomes more concentrated.

cards.q: What are the two caveats attached to the entropy/concentration measures?
cards.a: The normalisation depends on $$|E_T^+|$$, so runs using very different numbers of edges are not strictly comparable; and concentration is not congestion — a concentrated flow at low load can cause no delay at all, so the two are reported as separate outcomes.

cards.q: Write the system-level criterion $$\mathcal{J}(F,\pi)$$, and explain why throughput is excluded from it.
cards.a: $$\mathcal{J}(F,\pi) = q_{svc}\mathbb{E}[\bar\zeta_T] + q_{mov}\mathbb{E}[\bar{c}_T] + q_{wait}\mathbb{E}[W_T] + q_{conc}\mathbb{E}[C_T] + q_{back}\mathbb{E}[B_T]$$, all weights $$q_\bullet \ge 0$$. Throughput is excluded because it is maximisation-oriented and, under a fixed arrival rate, largely redundant with $$\bar\zeta_T$$ — including it with a negative weight would double-count; it is reported separately instead.

cards.q: [Fix, revised] $$W_T$$ appeared with no formula. What is it, and why isn't it just queueing delay $$(y_j-r_j)$$?
cards.a: A first pass defined $$W_T$$ as mean pre-assignment queueing delay, but that's largely redundant with the backlog term $$B_T$$ already in $$\mathcal{J}$$. Revised: $$W_T$$ measures time lost *after* assignment — $$W_T = \dfrac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_T|}\sum_{\tau_j\in\mathcal{C}_T}\sum_{t=y_j}^{d_j-1}\omega_j(t)$$, where $$\omega_j(t)\in\{0,1\}$$ flags the serving agent choosing wait or being overridden by the conflict-resolution operator. Not redundant with $$B_T$$, and distinct from $$\hat w_t(e)$$ (forward-looking, only feeds $$F$$).

cards.q: Where does the $$\omega_j(t)$$ flag inside $$W_T$$ actually come from operationally?
cards.a: It's the same override flag the conflict-resolution operator (Method §method:resolution) already sets when it forces an agent to wait instead of its proposed move — logged once, used twice: it defines $$\omega_j(t)$$ for $$W_T$$, and it's the $$\mathbb{1}[a_i\text{ overridden at }t]$$ term in the reward (Method eq:reward). No separate instrumentation needed.

cards.q: State the formal decision problem $$(F^\star,\pi^\star)$$ and note its status in the thesis.
cards.a: $$(F^\star,\pi^\star) \in \arg\min_{F\in\mathcal{F},\,\pi\in\Pi} \mathcal{J}(F,\pi)$$ subject to the feasible-storage, transition, vertex-conflict, swap-conflict and coupling constraints. It is a framing device: the thesis does not solve it globally, only estimates the effect of selected $$(F,\pi)$$ combinations under a factorial design.

cards.q: [Fix] Do the vertex-conflict and swap-conflict constraints actually restrict the search over $$\pi\in\Pi$$ in the decision problem?
cards.a: No, not really — and this is now stated explicitly. Those constraints are enforced by a resolution mechanism applied identically regardless of which $$\pi$$ is chosen, so they hold for *every* $$\pi\in\Pi$$ automatically. They're listed in eq. 25 to state explicitly that a solution is a claim about feasible *realised trajectories*, not because any candidate $$(F,\pi)$$ could violate them — unlike the feasible-storage and coupling constraints, which genuinely do restrict $$F$$ and the task stream.

cards.q: State the thesis's formal research question.
cards.a: Whether there exists an adaptive storage rule $$F$$ such that $$\mathcal{J}(F,\pi) < \mathcal{J}(F_{fix},\pi)$$ by a margin exceeding seed variance, and whether the size of that margin depends on the controller's information regime and on the load parameters $$m$$ and $$\lambda_{task}$$.

cards.q: What agent-level simplifications does the model make?
cards.a: Agents are homogeneous, occupy exactly one vertex, and carry at most one task at a time. There is no capacity, battery, or kinematic model — turning and acceleration costs are absorbed into the edge cost $$c(e)$$.

cards.q: In what sense is execution deterministic, and where does the model's stochasticity actually come from?
cards.a: An accepted action always succeeds, so the transition kernel $$P$$ is stochastic only through order arrivals — not through execution noise or failed moves.

cards.q: [Fix] The conflict-resolution mechanism decides who yields when two agents conflict — could that be a second source of randomness, undermining "deterministic execution"?
cards.a: It could have been (if resolution used randomised tie-breaking), but it doesn't: the fix states explicitly that the conflict-resolution mechanism is itself deterministic given the state, so it introduces no stochasticity beyond order arrivals — closing a gap where this was assumed but never confirmed.

cards.q: In what sense is inventory relocation "abstract" in this model?
cards.a: The storage update $$F$$ changes the placement template used to generate future tasks, but the physical movement of stock itself is never simulated; if $$\chi=0$$ in the storage objective, that (unsimulated) movement is also modelled as free.

cards.q: What does it mean that replenishment and depletion are "modelled only if stated"?
cards.a: By default, $$x_t$$ is treated purely as a placement template — not a physical stock level that depletes on pickup or is replenished over time — unless the study explicitly states otherwise.

cards.q: What two specific results does the thesis flag as conditional because of these scope limits?
cards.a: Results about the value of congestion feedback are conditional on relocation being cheap ($$\chi$$ small); results about decentralised control are conditional on execution being deterministic.

cards.q: What is the six-stage loop every controller architecture plugs into, and why does that matter?
cards.a: (1) orders → tasks enter $$\mathcal{Q}_t$$; (2) task assignment (shared across all three architectures); (3) routing (architecture-specific — this is the only stage that differs); (4) conflict resolution; (5) execution + logging; (6) storage update if it's a storage epoch. Because only stage 3 differs, a result difference is attributable to the routing architecture, not confounded with the rest of the pipeline.

cards.q: What are the three named storage rules (the "ladder"), and what does comparing the last two isolate?
cards.a: $$F_{fix}$$ (identity, already in Problem Formulation), $$F_{dem}$$ (demand-only greedy slotting), $$F_{cng}$$ (demand + congestion-aware). $$F_{dem}$$ vs $$F_{cng}$$ isolates exactly the thesis's core question: the value of *traffic* information over *demand* information alone.

cards.q: How is $$F_{dem}$$ realised concretely?
cards.a: Sort SKUs by demand estimate $$\hat\rho_t(k)$$ descending; sort storage vertices by distance to nearest delivery point ascending; place SKUs into vertices in that joint order, skipping vertices at capacity. This greedily solves the storage objective with $$\beta=\chi=0$$.

cards.q: How does $$F_{cng}$$ extend $$F_{dem}$$'s scoring?
cards.a: $$\mathrm{score}(k,v) = \hat\rho_t(k)\cdot d_G(v,\cdot) + \beta\sum_{e\in\mathrm{path}(v)}\hat\mu_t(e)\hat w_t(e)$$ — adds a congestion-exposure term along the access path; SKUs placed in ascending score order, same capacity check.

cards.q: How is the reassignment penalty $$R$$ actually realised, and why does that mean $$\chi$$ is never swept?
cards.a:
As a hard cap of $$
u$$ relocated units per epoch ($$R=0$$ if $$\le
u$$ relocations, $$R=\infty$$ otherwise), so any finite $$\chi>0$$ enforces it — $$\chi$$ is fixed, not tuned. Only the top-$$
u$$ highest-marginal-value relocations are applied, in strict descending order (ties: SKU id then vertex id) — this is also the tie-breaking rule Problem Formulation requires for $$F$$ to be a genuine function.

cards.q: How is task assignment (shared across all three controller architectures) realised?
cards.a: Greedy matching: for each waiting task in $$\mathcal{Q}_t$$ ordered oldest-first, assign the free agent minimising $$d_G(\ell_i(t), s_j)$$. Not the optimal (Hungarian) matching — that's a one-line ablation, not a change to $$\Pi$$.

cards.q: How does the section-based controller's zone-boundary protocol work, concretely?
cards.a: Each zone runs its own independent prioritised planner using only zone-local state. An agent whose route crosses a zone boundary yields to whichever zone currently has fewer active agents, ties broken by agent id — one explicit stated rule, not left implicit.

cards.q: Write the action-masking formula, and what does it guarantee?
cards.a: With $$d_{max}=\max_v|N^+(v)|$$, the policy outputs $$d_{max}+1$$ logits; at $$\ell_i(t)=v$$, logits outside $$\mathcal{U}(v)$$ are set to $$-\infty$$ before softmax. This makes each individual action legal *by construction*, not just in expectation — though it does NOT by itself make the *joint* action legal (that's the resolution operator's job).

cards.q: Write the reward function, and explain the theoretical guarantee behind its first term.
cards.a: $$R_i(t) = \gamma\Phi_i(t{+}1)-\Phi_i(t) + r_{deliver}\mathbb{1}[\text{completes task}] - r_{blk}\mathbb{1}[\text{overridden}] - r_{cng}\delta_i(t)$$, with $$\Phi_i(t)=-\eta_i(\ell_i(t),t)$$. The first term is potential-based shaping (Ng et al. 1999): provably doesn't alter the game's equilibria, extended to *dynamic* potentials (Devlin & Kudenko 2012) — needed since $$\Phi_i$$ is non-stationary by construction (target changes at every reassignment).

cards.q: Why must $$r_{blk}$$ not be finalised before the conflict-resolution operator is verified?
cards.a: The penalty is meaningless until overrides are detected correctly — a mis-scaled feasibility penalty is one of the most common causes of a MAPF policy that learns to just stand still.

cards.q: Is the $$-r_{cng}\delta_i(t)$$ reward term also potential-based shaping?
cards.a: No — it's a plain per-step penalty, not shaping. Unlike the progress term, it can in principle shift the equilibrium. Stated as an accepted, deliberate trade-off for giving the policy a direct congestion-avoidance signal, not an oversight.

cards.q: How does the encoder build the agent embedding $$z_i$$ from the local observation?
cards.a: $$Q$$ rounds of message passing over node features: $$m_v^{(q)}=\phi_q(h_v^{(q-1)}, \{h_w^{(q-1)}\})$$, $$h_v^{(q)}=\psi_q(h_v^{(q-1)}, m_v^{(q)})$$. Then $$z_i$$ concatenates the agent's own final-layer embedding, an aggregation of incoming messages from communicating agents, and $$\delta_i(t)$$.

cards.q: What's the honest caveat about using $$Q=0$$ as a "no-communication" ablation?
cards.a: $$Q=0$$ collapses message passing entirely, ablating *both* local structural propagation within $$\mathcal{G}_i^{(d)}(t)$$ *and* inter-agent communication at once — it doesn't cleanly isolate communication alone. A cleaner fix would use two separate round-counts; noted as an open refinement, not adopted in the skeleton.

cards.q: Describe the conflict-resolution algorithm precisely.
cards.a: A priority permutation of agents is drawn once per episode from the episode seed. Agents are processed in that fixed order; each agent's proposed move is accepted if it doesn't conflict with the already-finalised successors of higher-priority agents; otherwise it's overridden to wait, and flagged.

cards.q: Why does this operator always terminate in a feasible joint action, and why does that matter for the Scope section's determinism claim?
cards.a: Waiting never conflicts with an already-finalised successor except by occupying the current vertex — impossible, since the prior joint state was itself collision-free. This determinism is exactly what *licenses* Problem Formulation's Scope claim that execution introduces no stochasticity beyond order arrivals — the claim holds because of this construction, not independently of it.

cards.q: What two storage-training regimes are distinguished, and why does one matter more?
cards.a: Training under $$F_{fix}$$ only (then evaluated against all three storage rules) vs. "matched" training (same rule at train and eval). Matched training under an adaptive $$F$$ is harder: it makes the task distribution non-stationary from the learner's perspective, since the coupling condition routes pickups differently as $$x_t$$ changes underneath the policy.

cards.q: Why precompute all-pairs shortest paths once per instance rather than on demand?
cards.a: $$G$$ is static, and $$d_G$$ is queried every single timestep by both the observation builder ($$\eta_i$$) and the storage rule ($$F_{cng}$$'s score) — recomputing repeatedly would be wasteful.

cards.q: Why must the order generator ($$P_{ord}$$) be seeded separately from the policy and environment?
cards.a: So the exact same order stream replays identically under every controller and storage rule — which is what makes the paired $$(F,\pi)$$ comparison in the formal research question actually meaningful (same task stream, different treatment).

cards.q: What are the four correctness assertions run on *every* experiment, not just once in development?
cards.a: (1) no vertex/swap conflict on the realised trace; (2) every realised storage configuration lies in $$\mathcal{X}$$; (3) every released task is in exactly one of $$\mathcal{Q}_t,\mathcal{B}_t,\mathcal{C}_t$$ at every timestep; (4) bitwise replay determinism under fixed seeds.

cards.q: How is $$W_T$$ operationalised in Implementation without needing separate instrumentation?
cards.a: It reuses the conflict-resolution operator's override flag directly: one bit per timestep, logged for whichever agent is serving an active task, summed per task. That same flag also drives the reward's override penalty $$r_{blk}$$ — one piece of instrumentation, two uses.

cards.q: At a high level, what did the technical review of the Problem Formulation find?
cards.a: One genuine mathematical error (the target-distance potential's shortest-path claim was overstated), plus about a dozen definitional gaps where the section was less formal than it looked (undefined $$\Pi$$/$$\mathcal{F}$$, a task tuple missing its SKU, no initial storage state, task-lifecycle sets only described narratively, etc.), plus some pure notation-clarity issues. See `GAPS.md` and `problem_formulation_fixed.tex` in the repo for the full write-up and concrete fixes.

cards.q: What was the one place a formally stated property was actually mathematically false, not just underspecified?
cards.a: The claim that the potential difference $$\eta_i(w,t)-\eta_i(v,t)$$ is "negative exactly on shortest-path moves." By the triangle inequality it's only guaranteed that the difference is $$\ge -c(v,w)$$, with equality (not mere negativity) iff the move is on a shortest path. A negative-but-not-equal difference is a real counterexample.

cards.q: Which symbol families in the formulation are visually confusable, and why weren't they renamed?
cards.a: The "C" family ($$c(e)$$, $$\hat c$$, $$\bar c_T$$, $$C_T$$, $$\mathcal{C}_t$$ — five unrelated concepts), the "Q" family ($$\mathcal{Q}_t$$, $$q_i(t)$$, $$q_{svc}$$ etc.), and $$\mathcal{O}_i$$ vs $$O_i$$. Not renamed because that would require touching the Method/Implementation sections too (which weren't reviewed) — instead, a "Notation used more than once" table was added to the fixed .tex disambiguating them in one place.

cards.q: Which issues were deliberately left open rather than fixed in the revised draft, and why?
cards.a: (1) $$m$$ used in §A before being defined in §B — fixed with a one-line forward pointer, not full reordering. (2) Full renaming of C/Q/O-family symbols — flagged via a table, not executed (thesis-wide change). (3) No unit/scale normalisation is discussed for the five unlike-unit terms summed in $$\mathcal{J}(F,\pi)$$ — a Method-level calibration concern, not a Problem Formulation error, but worth raising if asked how the weights $$q_\bullet$$ were chosen.

cards.q: Two gaps involved objects used before being formally connected to anything. What were they?
cards.a: The congestion feature $$\delta_i(t)$$ (defined in the Learning Problem section but never added to the observation tuple $$o_i(t)$$ or to $$R_i$$), and the SKU $$k_j$$ (used in the coupling condition but never made part of the task tuple $$\tau_j$$). Both are now wired into their proper definitions.

cards.q: If an examiner asks "why keep constraints in eq. 25 that are always satisfied anyway?" — what's the one-line answer?
cards.a: They're not there to prune the search over $$\pi$$ (a separate resolution mechanism guarantees them for every $$\pi$$) — they're there to state explicitly that a claimed solution $$(F^\star,\pi^\star)$$ is a statement about feasible *realised trajectories*, which is a different (and necessary) kind of claim from "this $$\pi$$ minimises $$\mathcal{J}$$."

cards.q: Two definitions (task lifecycle sets, and $$F$$ via the storage objective) had the same underlying issue: a descriptive/set-valued definition standing in for a function. How was each fixed?
cards.a: $$\mathcal{Q}_t,\mathcal{B}_t,\mathcal{C}_t$$: replaced narrative description with explicit interval-based set-builder definitions using a new assignment-time symbol $$y_j$$, making disjointness a consequence rather than an assertion. $$F$$: added a requirement that ties break via a fixed rule over the $$\arg\min$$'s minimising set, so eq. 7 is a genuine function.

cards.q: Where should you look for the full, citable version of this review?
cards.a: `GAPS.tex` (repo root — a compilable LaTeX document, not markdown) has the full write-up per gap with severity (Error/Gap/Deviation/Clarity) and rationale, plus the comparison against Knippenberg et al. (2021); `problem_formulation_fixed.tex` and `method_implementation_skeleton.tex` are complete drop-in Sections IV and V–VI with every fix applied inline and tagged `% [Gxx]`/`% [Kxx]`, sharing labels so nothing breaks across files.

cards.q: [K1] What's the one connectivity assumption Knippenberg et al. (2021) state that this thesis's Problem Formulation only states a weaker version of?
cards.a: K21 assumes environment graphs are *strongly connected* outright — simple, crisp, easy to verify. The fixed Problem Formulation instead only requires $$d_G$$ to be finite for pairs actually used, which is weaker but more permissive of unreachable side-rooms/maintenance spurs. Framed as a deliberate judgement call, not a correctness fix: if generated instances never exercise a disconnected pocket, the stronger K21-style assumption should probably just be adopted outright.

cards.q: [K2] What is the single biggest gap the Knippenberg et al. (2021) comparison surfaced?
cards.a: K21's entire contribution is *time-constrained* MAPF — an explicit per-job deadline, either a hard feasibility cut or a soft penalty term in the objective. This thesis's task tuple carries only a release time $$r_j$$, no deadline — lateness only shows up as an aggregate average ($$\bar\zeta_T$$), never as a per-task failure. Since the thesis reuses K21's architecture (built specifically for deadlines) while dropping deadlines, this needed to be an explicit stated exclusion, not a silent omission — now fixed as one paragraph in Scope, naming exactly what re-adding a deadline $$t_j^d$$ would require.

cards.q: What did the Knippenberg comparison find that the thesis does *better* than its source, not just differently?
cards.a: Three things: (1) the dynamic, reassignment-driven target distance $$\eta_i$$ — K21's version is static per-episode and didn't need to handle a changing goal; (2) tighter conflict constraints — one inequality each for vertex/swap conflict, vs. K21's two-case prose definition with an extra "bidirectional edge" caveat that falls out for free here from constraint composition; (3) potential-based reward shaping (Method) vs. K21's ad hoc fixed-magnitude reward table — and PPO instead of DQN, which is literally what K21's own Future Work section asked for.
